extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, public opinion, and constitutional history
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the institutional, informational, and social conditions that shape public opinion and the functioning of democratic institutions (e.g., self-contained communities, patronage, congressional information deficits, and proposals like guild socialism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained community shaping public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: In a self-contained township every citizen is assumed to be omnicompetent, public-spirited, and to share a homogeneous moral code; thus public opinion is based chiefly on a few stereotyped images and local experiences rather than broad objective reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains rotation in office by 'jacks of all trades', the limited sources of information (few newspapers, pamphlets, speeches, rumor), and that disagreements are confined to local application of shared standards. Anti-pattern: projecting the village model onto a complex civilization produces static, stereotyped public opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires instruments of knowledge (news/common language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic theory depends on instruments for reporting the environment — free circulation of news and a common language — without which citizens must fall back on local wisdom and stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The founders could not conceive an organization of knowledge enabling simultaneous common facts across communities; the absence of such instruments forced reliance on local conscience and legal/moral codes. Evaluation should consider the extent of information circulation and shared discourse in a polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of legalism and deduction from absolute principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When communities lack instruments for empirical knowledge, they tend to rely on deduction from fixed legal and moral formulas, producing static theorism rather than practical, experience-based policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts dynamic practical energy of people with static public-life theorism; criterion for assessment is whether a polity substitutes tested rules for experiential learning, leading to rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to neutralize local opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional doctrine of checks and balances (making 'ambition counteract ambition') is designed to offset self-centered local interests and prevent local or class preferences from obstructing national governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founders framed machinery (Senate, electoral college, veto, judicial interpretation) to deadlock and equilibrate interests rather than produce perpetual gridlock. Use this criterion to judge institutional designs intended to balance competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and rotation in office as stabilizing yet distorting forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office and patronage were promoted as democratic reforms to abolish office monopoly, but in large polities they often create a permanent governing class and serve to attach local leaders to national power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes the intended benefits (prevent bureaucracy, open careers) and unintended consequences (professional politicians, oscillation of offices among henchmen). Evaluation should weigh democratic legitimacy against practical stabilization effects of patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government needs systematic information systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature (e.g., Congress) without systematic, adequate, and authorized means of knowing national circumstances is effectively a 'group of blind men' whose combination of local impressions is insufficient for national policy-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include legislation produced by insiders or broken into local items, reliance on logrolling and pork, and episodic investigative mania. Criterion: presence/absence of institutional mechanisms for reliable national information and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive advantage via control of administrative information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presidency gains power because the executive presides over a vast collection of bureaus and agents that gather information and can choose what to present to the legislature, producing a one-sided relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text highlights that presidents can 'tell Congress what he chooses to tell it', making legislative reliance on executive-supplied facts and occasional private leaks or newspaper enterprise. Evaluate concentration of informational control in the executive branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logrolling and pork as symptoms of informational deficits
rubrics_metrics.description: When legislators lack broad factual grounding, they specialize on few issues and rely on logrolling and the distribution of local benefits (tariff schedules, naval yards, post offices) to satisfy constituents rather than craft coherent national policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should identify whether policy is produced as aggregations of local items and whether logrolling substitutes for substantive legislative deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of common consciousness determines reliance on force vs. patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: In associations among large groups (federal unions, industrial governments), the extent to which material/common consciousness exists determines whether cooperation depends on physical force or on milder alternatives like patronage and privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'secret of great state-builders' is to calculate this; use this principle to evaluate why some polities use coercion while others use patronage to secure cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guild socialism's Commune: enumerated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Guild Socialism the Commune (federal structure of local/provincial communes with a national commune) is assigned wide powers: settling/fixing prices, allocating surplus/loss, allocating natural resources and credit, allocating communal labor-power, ratifying guild budgets and by-laws, levying taxes, allocating income to non-productive members, appointing judges, conferring coercive powers, declaring war and making peace, controlling armed forces, running police, and regulating personal conduct and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book reproduces Cole's list almost verbatim; this serves as a checklist to evaluate whether a proposed functional/communal institution is effectively sovereign and coercive despite claims of non-coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim vs reality: non-coercive polity may still be coercive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a system (e.g., Guild Socialism) is touted as 'not an instrument of coercion' and 'conceived in the spirit of free service', the institutional powers it reserves (see Commune's powers) amount to coercive authority indistinguishable from state sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to interrogate reform proposals that claim to reduce coercion: enumerate powers and ask whether coercive mechanisms remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions to new social orders require force or direct action
rubrics_metrics.description: Cole and other reformers acknowledge that establishing a guild society cannot be achieved by universal consent; transition would require a period of force or direct action (e.g., trade union direct action, possible civil conflict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate feasibility of systemic change by examining whether proponents account for the means of transition and the role of coercion in that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of capitalist property alone does not guarantee non-coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Marxian diagnosis that removing capitalist property removes motives to aggression is insufficient: post-revolution governance still raises questions about how society will be run (state collectivism, guilds, cooperative societies, democratic parliament, or functional representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must consider institutional design for representation and administration after structural economic change; eliminating property relations is not a full solution to coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation between centralization and decentralization involves coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical reformers alternate between centralization (empire/Roman peace) and decentralization (autonomy/self-sufficiency), but both choices entail coercion — centralized rule coerces at center, decentralization leads to local conflicts requiring defense or arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to evaluate proposals by asking which form reduces coercion in practice and how defense/conflict resolution will be organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric and public perception can rewrite constitutional meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Political leaders and movements (e.g., Jefferson) can recast a constitution's character through rhetoric and practice, transforming an undemocratic text into a perceived democratic instrument and thereby altering political norms and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing constitutional legitimacy or meaning, consider both formal text and dominant public narratives/stereotypes that reshape interpretation over time.
